title: Does Masonry help musicians' lives? Joppa Lodge and Harlem Lodge
summary: Caldwell thinks the principles help; Hodges, Carney and Procope belonged to Joppa 55, and he served as a grand lodge officer in the 1960s.

story.theme_name: The musicians' union: cards, locals, and the Black-white merger
story.community_name: The musicians' union: cards, scale and the black-white merger

blocks.x: Well, do you think that -- I mean
would you say from your experience -- I mean you know a lot of musicians in other lodges -- do you think that the principles or precepts of masonry have helped their lives?
Yeah, because a lot of them admit it.
Yes, because I was just trying to think that --
A lot of them admit it.
-- those I know, they must be fairly, they -- you don't hear of them getting into any trouble.
Well, which lodge were those people like Johnny Hodges in?

Johnny belonged to Joppa 55 -- Johnny, Carney, Procop, they joined over there in Joppa 55. They the one that gave Duke, his a masonic funeral too because Duke's mother lodge was in Washington, D. C., but most all these fellows here, they're all living except some that deceased (unintelligible) on the communication, but most of the big ones outside of Joppa -- but Harlem Lodge carry more than anybody. I guess about all the doctors up there together, about 30 some lodges.
What would the population up there be, do you reckon? I mean do they have --

They have around about 5,000, more than that now, the last one I remember, and I was appointed by the grand master to serve at the junior grand master of ceremonies in '64 and '66. Harrison Clark, I was practically right hand man to him, and that time we had about -- maybe run about 7,000 or more. That's just one district, but they go by districts. See, like in Brooklyn's the second masonic district. And like Mount Vernon is the third, on up the scale, you know, third, fourth, fifth, sixth, seventh, eighth, all the way up.
